title: Separate luck, complicity and responsibility in a hard case

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Moral luck separates an action’s foreseeable risk from its eventual consequence. Complicity asks how participation, benefit or omission connects someone to a harmful arrangement. A dirty-hands case has no feasible harmless option; ordinary avoidable negligence is different.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Two volunteers each ignore an available cover instruction. One borrowed item stays dry by chance; the other suffers 20 units of damage. Both had time and a cover. The organizer omitted a known nearby shelter from the plan. Separately, a room closure forces a coordinator to cancel either a promised youth meeting or a promised adult support meeting; only one equally suitable accessible room remains, both groups rely on it, and no rescheduling option exists today. Both groups can be told immediately.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Compare culpable conduct and actual repair in the rain case, then analyze the unavoidable conflict without calling either group worthless. Identify whose role controls each decision.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A member benefits from a rule excluding newcomers but neither made it nor can change it alone. Are total innocence and total responsibility the only options?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Both volunteers neglected the same precaution, but only one item needs the supplied damage repair; the organizer’s omission is separate. The closure case retains an unavoidable broken expectation even after a defensible selection and prompt notice. A fair prior allocation rule or reasoned urgent-need distinction may help, but no supplied fact chooses a unique winner. Partial: report only outcomes. Incorrect: say the lucky volunteer acted well or every participant bears equal blame.
criteria: Unavoidable residual harm is not erased

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Examine knowledge, actual benefit, available influence and cost of refusal. The member may raise a reasoned change or stop an avoidable contribution to harm; receiving a benefit does not alone establish equal responsibility with the rule-maker.
criteria: Unavoidable residual harm is not erased
